lines: A function is marked unsafe and ships with a documented contract.
Does calling it from behind a real safe guard that checks the contract first ever reach undefined behavior?
answer: A real, enforcing guard keeps it sound.

lines: Run it for real: every real call that genuinely satisfies the documented contract returns the genuinely correct value, every single time.
Now send the guard three requests outside the real contract.
Does it still let any of them reach the unsafe code underneath it?
answer: Every one is rejected before the unsafe code ever runs.

lines: Run it for real: the real guard genuinely rejected every one of the three out-of-contract requests, and the unsafe function's own real call counter never moved for them.
steps.takeaway: Soundness means a guard rejects every out-of-contract call, not merely most of them.

lines: Suppose a different caller skipped the guard and called the unsafe function directly, with the identical invalid inputs.
Would that genuinely violate the documented contract?
answer: That's exactly outside the documented bound.

lines: Run it for real: the identical invalid inputs genuinely violate the real documented contract, the exact real bound the guard above was built to enforce.
steps.takeaway: My callers don't misuse it is weaker than a guard that genuinely cannot be misused.

lines: Two real, independent sources on this exact rule agree, in their own words.
Unsafe code is sound only if no safe caller can ever trigger undefined behavior through it, and a real Safety section is how that contract gets written down.
steps.takeaway: A documented contract plus a real, enforcing guard is the whole of what soundness asks for.

lines: So here's why the word unsafe is misleading if you read it as a speed setting: nothing about the keyword itself removes a single rule Rust enforces everywhere else, it only moves the job of proving those rules onto the person who wrote that one function.

That's also why a comment claiming something runs faster is never, on its own, a safety argument: faster and sound are answering two completely different questions, and this topic's own guard shows what actually answering the second one looks like in real code.

And the sharper standard underneath all of it is the one this topic measured directly: it isn't enough that today's callers happen to behave, since a function is only sound once no caller, however it is written, can ever reach the broken state through the safe surface alone.
